What's funny about this, is that not everyone can reproduce it.

I can on both my desktop and under a virtual machine, but a friend (who also uses OpenBSD) cannot. We have tried a few different `LC_CTYPE`s and `TERMs` and even different terminals, but thus far have not been able to figure this out...

Do the neovim devs have any ideas?

For the lua tests we set LC_ALL : https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/7087/commits/5c08c8c00969b8945f1351f49b0afb7e3e8842fe

Maybe we need to do that for oldtest (`src/nvim/testdir`) as well. (I didn't check if we already try to, somewhere.)
I'll give that a go, thanks.

Hrm, I'm running the tests for a port Makefile like this:

```
do-test:
        cd ${WRKSRC} && env LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 ${MAKE_PROGRAM} \
                -C src/nvim/testdir NVIM_PRG=${WRKBUILD}/bin/nvim ${MAKE_FLAGS}
```

```

TEST FAILURE
```

Could be useful to compare ktraces for a successful execution of that specific test and a failing one.

I probably won't be able to look into this until after next week.

Sorry, I had to delete my ktrace as it contained the contents of files that I had been editing, including emails. That's scary. No idea why that kind of thing should be in the trace!
Anyway, this suggests that nvim is not running in a clean environment. Could this be the issue?

I did the same as @vext01  and decided to remove the file - why does neovim touch those files on startup? It seems to be chunking them in with mmap, is there a purpose for this?

EDIT: found out what it it - it's documented in `:help shada`
Yup, `shada` is an improved `viminfo`, which is used by Vim. If you don't want it, put `set shada=` in your vimrc or disable it only temporarily via `nvim -i NONE`.

OK, here's why mulander didn't see the test failure:

```
  if executable('bash')
    set shell=bash
  elseif executable('zsh')
    set shell=zsh
  else
    return
  endif
```

He had neither bash, nor zsh installed. He was using ksh.

So this test just fails on OpenBSD.

FWIW, I have both installed. The test twill use bash.

I'm using:
```
GNU bash, version 4.4.12(1)-release (x86_64-unknown-openbsd6.2)
```

```
$ vim --cmd "so before.vim" <(cat Xtestin)
```

I see in the status area:

```
"/dev/fd/11" is not a file
````

I was really surprised to see that this file exists on my OpenBSD laptop. I've never heard of `/dev/fd/*`:

```
$ file /dev/fd/11
/dev/fd/11: character special (22/11)
```

I'm not really sure why you would use these device nodes instead of a plain `open()` syscall, but it seems to be something wrong with the nvim code that opens/reads these dev nodes.

Incremental progress...

> I'm not really sure why you would use these device nodes

It's testing detection of encoding when reading from a fifo.  That's why it's going through the hassle of using `<(cat Xtestin)`.



> "/dev/fd/11" is not a file

This shouldn't be happening.  That means that [this code](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/d9b3ebfede6439aab4148c4bbf117b8950ed6aa0/src/nvim/fileio.c#L434-L436) isn't considering that a fifo.

When I run `stat -L <(ls)` on my Linux system, it says the file is a fifo.  Is there an equivalent for OpenBSD?
Also, does Vim's own test succeed?

> Quick test of /dev/fd/* to check for the possibility that it's bust on OpenBSD

That's not testing the same thing.  The test isn't whether Vim can open `/dev/fd/...`.  That filename is an implementation detail of the command substitution (`<(ls)`) that the shell is performing.

The test is checking whether (n)vim can properly detecting the encoding when editing a _fifo_.

> Vim's own test? You mean regular vim?

Correct.

From a git clone, you can run the test with `make && make -C src/testdir test_startup_utf8.res`.

Then `cat src/testdir/messages` will show the results.
What does `stat -L -f "%N: %HT%SY" <(ls)` show?
os_nodetype was recently changed (it should behave exactly like vim now....). Does reverting it to the 0.2 0 version fix the issue?
